title: The Thinking Leakage in Reinforcement Learning for LLMs
titleEn: Thought leakage in reinforcement learning for large language models
summary: The paper trains Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B with GRPO in no-thinking mode, proposing that a large part of the accuracy improvement comes from thought leakage, i.e., reactivating the model's original reasoning ability from thinking mode, rather than learning new problem-solving behavior. During training, responses became longer and reflection words increased; the original model judged them as more thinking-like, reaching 94% on 8B, with internal activations shifting 0.56 toward the thinking direction. Intervention experiments show that scaling RL weight updates pushes the model toward thinking mode but does not exceed its accuracy; replacing the 8-dimensional thinking subspace removes 75% of the gain, reverse replacement transfers 50%, and the change goes through attention heads that read empty think blocks. The authors trace the source of this optimization pressure to GRPO advantage signals favoring thinking-like responses.

parts.text: Hybrid reasoning models trained via RLVR in no-think mode often show improved reasoning accuracy. This paper investigates whether this gain comes from the model learning new problem-solving abilities or merely reactivating reasoning capabilities already present in the model from pretraining or the original think mode (thinking leakage).
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: The authors trained Qwen3 models with GRPO in no-think mode and designed causal intervention experiments at three levels: weights, activations, and attention heads, testing the mechanism through weight difference scaling, cross-model exchange of the 8-dimensional think activation subspace, and ablation and patching of key attention heads that read the empty thinking block.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: On Qwen3-8B, replacing the 8-dimensional think subspace eliminated 75% of the RL gain, while backporting transferred 50% of the gain; a few attention heads that read the empty think block carried most of the pattern-shift signal; the GRPO advantage function naturally assigns stronger positive updates to answers with more think-like features.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: Limitations: only drawn from question 5; weight scaling hyperparameters were not validated on a held-out test set; experiments only covered Qwen3 1.7B, 4B, and 8B models and 90 AIME math problems; the paper does not report generalization to multi-turn dialogue, other task domains, or other model architectures.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: 论文审计 LLM 裁判可靠性：重复一致不等于正确
AutoEnvScaling: Automating the Data Flywheel with Terminal Agents
titleEn: AutoEnvScaling: Automating the Data Flywheel with Terminal Agents
summary: The paper proposes AutoEnvScaling, which treats RL environment design as a terminal task, where a proposer agent generates new environments based on the rollouts of the solver being trained, and the solver's new rollouts then drive the next round. The authors report that compared to prompt-only generation, the effective environment rate improves by up to 25 times, and the cost per effective environment decreases by up to 75%. Training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with AutoEnvScaling environments generated by GPT-5.6-sol yields a Terminal-Bench 2.1 score 4.3 points higher than the matched Tmax baseline; when Qwen3.6-35B-A3B serves as both proposer and solver, Terminal-Bench 2.1 improves by 12.2 points, and Terminal-Bench 4.0 rises from 1.6 to 3.2.

parts.text: Reinforcement learning for terminal agents needs diverse, verifiable environments, but these are still mostly designed by researchers, supply grows only with human effort, and they become obsolete once learned.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: AutoEnvScaling turns environment creation into a terminal task. The proposer writes and tests Harbor environments in a sandbox based on solver trajectories, validates and calibrates them before adding to the library, and new trajectories drive the next round; the same model can also serve both roles.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Across eight frontier proposers, terminal-style generation achieves the highest effective environment rates. When GPT-5.6-sol creates environments, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's TB2.1 is 4.3 points above matched Tmax. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B serves both roles, and TB2.1 goes from 41.1 to 53.3.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors state that whether gains persist over longer training has not been established, TB4.0 remains low, and passing validation does not guarantee environment correctness. Cross-domain experiments go up to generation and admission, and downstream training gains in these domains have not been shown, according to the authors.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Cortex: Measurement-Gated Evolution and Pruning of Coding-Agent Skills and Rules
titleEn: Cortex: Measurement-Gated Evolution and Pruning of Coding-Agent Skills and Rules

title: 研究：事实核查评测可能混入声明时不可知的未来证据
titleEn: Research: fact-checking evaluations may mix in future evidence unknowable at the time of the claim
summary: Researchers reconstructed the evidence conditions at the time of claim creation on AVeriTeC and QuanTemp++, and probed model representations for encoded outcome information, finding clear parametric leakage that is masked by overall accuracy. The authors state that a simple representation bottleneck reduces such future information leakage more effectively than mutual information-based training penalties. The study also found that allowing evidence published after the claim inflates AVeriTeC zero-shot accuracy by 6.3 percentage points, while the effect is negligible on QuanTemp++, where retrieval provides almost no post-hoc evidence. The authors conclude that misinformation benchmarks overestimate fact-checking performance if they do not account for information actually available at the time of the claim.

parts.text: Fact-checking benchmarks often count information unknowable at the time of the claim as success. The parameter channel is the outcome memorized during pretraining; the temporal channel is retrieved evidence published after the claim. The authors argue that a single accuracy score cannot distinguish these two paths.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Recover the publication date on AVeriTeC and QuanTemp++, split into point-in-time and leaked views. Entity obfuscation tests the parameter channel, with the control being GPT-2-XL truncated at December 2017. On frozen Qwen3-14B, compare width bottleneck against CLUB penalty.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Qwen3-14B after occlusion: Supported recall 0.421→0.131, accuracy drops 0.032; control reverses. AVeriTeC post-hoc evidence raises zero-shot by 6.3 points; with prior evidence +0.031. QuanTemp++ difference 0.05% (p=0.87).
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors state that outcome information cannot be said to be completely removed: date coverage is incomplete, no manual spot checks were done, and the two date tools differ. The training detector uses only Qwen3-14B, with features processed via mean-pooling and PCA. Next, they will test claims after the training cutoff and check whether high-quality evidence exists before the claim.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models
titleEn: RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models
summary: The paper proposes RSI-Anything, a domain-general framework built on JEPA-Anything, which uses predictive world models to guide action and training data selection for recursive self-improvement; observed feedback drives policy or workflow improvements and conditional world model adaptation, while component and compatibility checks determine whether to retain the updated policy-model combination. In code repair tasks, with a fixed coder, the success rate improves from 26.3% with a static verifier to 29.2% with predictive selection, reaching 31.2% after world model adaptation, with comparable test usage. In GUI evaluation, task completion rates are higher, with average action count reduced by 39.4%; laboratory planning scores more than double from 21.80% to 46.01% across five consecutive policy versions. In reaction optimization, under the same budget of 40 experiments, RSI-Anything achieves an average optimal yield of 96.15%, compared to 82.16% for Bayesian optimization. The paper also presents an end-to-end immunology application, connecting workflow evolution and predictive modeling to therapeutic hypothesis generation.

parts.text: Recursive self-improvement requires one round of interaction experience to improve the next round's actions and learning, and the updates must be retained. External feedback requires executing the candidate before the consequences are known, and the budget is limited; policy updates also change the candidate distribution the world model faces.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: RSI-Anything uses the world model from JEPA-Anything to score candidates and decide who gets external evaluation. Feedback drives policy or workflow updates, and adapts the world model when reliability, data, and budget allow; component checks and compatibility checks decide which pair is kept.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: With the coder fixed, CodeContests hidden-test all-pass rates go from 26.3% to 31.2% (static verifier to world-model adaptation). Five versions of 4B F200 Level-2 go from 21.80% to 46.01%. Across 40 streaming experiments, the average best yield is 96.15%, versus 82.16% for the control.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors say that joint multi-round evaluation of the policy and world model within the same task is still needed; the lab results evaluate protocol-aligned planning, and the treatment hypothesis awaits experimental testing. The code fix keeps the coder fixed, and OSWorld does not report absolute success rates.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
titleEn: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Execution Framework Improvement for Open Worlds
summary: The paper proposes Harness^2, a pluggable recursive agent execution framework improvement method that automatically edits the execution framework in open-world tasks lacking ground-truth verifiers through two levels of recursion: task-level and improvement-level. Task-level recursion uses contrastive Propose-Probe-Compose steps to guide edits, extendable with parallel or serial recursion; improvement-level recursion extracts experience from these edits to update a continuous improvement framework, better adapting the agent to future tasks. Across three specialized benchmarks and four model-framework configurations, single-step recursion improves GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash relative to the base framework, with WorkBuddy-Bench improving by up to 11.5 points, JobBench by 4.5 points, and LAB by 11.8 percentage points, and further improvements with increased task-level recursion budget.

parts.text: Open-world tasks are typically unseen at design time, and there is no ground-truth verifier at test time; only modifying the current task or inheriting a custom execution harness both struggle to reliably serve future tasks. The authors want to simultaneously improve the current harness and how the harness will be improved in the future.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Task level uses Propose–Probe–Compose: propose invariant and domain candidates, compare behavioral differences under matched conditions, then compose; the budget can be expanded in parallel or sequentially. After the task, write experience supported by execution comparison into the improvement library. The next question still starts from the initial harness, guided by the library; weights are not updated.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: All four configurations are above base in a single step. The authors state that on WB, GLM-5+OpenCode single-step gains +11.5 points, and JobBench and LAB Partial gain up to +4.5 points and +11.8 percentage points. k=5 adds more; LAB has one spot where Meta-Harness is higher.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors point out that recursion increases inference cost, only characterizes the trade-off within a bounded budget, and does not give a universally optimal allocation. Without ground truth, it relies on behavior comparison and model judgment, which does not guarantee correctness or transfer across tasks. The recursive form and budget need to be specified in advance. The main results are three shuffled-order streams on two executors, two initial harnesses, and three benchmarks.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: 论文用生成式 Agent 建模模拟私有测试集对评分与用户体验差距的影响
titleEn: Paper uses generative agents to model how private test sets affect the gap between scores and user experience
summary: An arXiv paper proposes a simulation architecture combining rule-based market dynamics with LLM-driven policy agents to study how benchmark design affects decisions by model providers, users, funders, and regulators. The authors model benchmarks, consumer demand, and provider capabilities as vectors over six capability dimensions: reasoning, programming, knowledge, safety, communication, and agents, and use benchmark held-out set design as a case study. The simulation finds that shifting from public benchmarks to private held-out benchmarks narrows the gap between scores and user satisfaction on most benchmarks, but widens it on a few, depending on which capabilities the held-out weights attribute scores to. The authors say the simulation can serve as a hypothesis-generation sandbox for studying how evaluation and policy choices reshape the ecosystem in turn.

parts.text: Benchmark scores guide R&D, capital, and regulation, but design methods often fix the rest of the ecosystem. The authors argue that evaluation should be treated as a closed loop, asking what the ecosystem does after a benchmark exists, using whether the holdout set is public as a case study.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: The authors build a hybrid generative multi-agent model. A six-dimensional vector represents capabilities, benchmark loadings, and consumer demand; LLMs only make monthly institutional allocations, while scoring and market use rules, and information is forced into three parts: public, private, and truth. The case compares five holdout settings.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: The authors report that from fully public to fully private, the absolute gap in LLM runs narrowed in 10 of 13 benchmarks and widened in 3, and this held for 10/10 seeds; for the heuristic it narrowed in 9/13. The authors state that widening occurred when the held-out weights shifted scoring credit toward dimensions where R&D was already concentrated.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors state that the mechanism depends on weight perturbation, a six-dimensional ontology, leaderboard competition, and model-defined satisfaction; dimension loadings are settings. The simulation does not predict real markets and needs to be tested on real leaderboards. The heuristic uses 50 seeds per condition, Sonnet 10, and Opus and GPT-5.5 each 3.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: EviScene: Beyond "Is It AI?" for Agentic Image Factuality Assessment
titleEn: EviScene: Agentic image factuality evaluation beyond "is it AI-generated"
summary: EviScene achieves 79.05% balanced accuracy and 52.26% strict evidence sufficiency rate (SESR) on 1,527 test images with Qwen3.5-9B, improving over the same-backbone base agent by 6.71 and 9.37 percentage points, respectively. This multimodal ReAct agent targets image factuality evaluation: given an image and a general verification instruction, it iteratively refines factual questions and aligns external evidence when no textual claim is present, outputting a supported or refuted verdict with an explanation. The expert-reviewed EviLens benchmark contains 10,174 images covering 12 types of factual errors; training uses teacher-trajectory supervised fine-tuning plus privileged same-policy self-distillation.

parts.text: Judging whether an image is AI-generated does not determine whether the depicted situation has factual support. When only an image and a generic verification instruction are given, with no textual claim, the system must output supported or refuted and explain using external evidence.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: EviLens contains 10,174 expert-reviewed images and twelve types of factual errors. EviScene uses ReAct to alternate visual inspection, retrieval, and evidence verification, and refines questions with new findings. Qwen3.5-9B is first SFT on 4,872 teacher trajectories, then PSD on verified decisions.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: On 1,527 test images, the trained Qwen3.5-9B achieves 79.05% BAcc and 52.26% SESR, higher than the same-backbone Base. The authors state that investigation improves SESR across five shared backbones; Gemini 3.1 Pro's BAcc does not increase. Without web search, SESR is 35.89%.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The paper does not specifically discuss limitations. Experiments compare direct judgment and EviScene on EviLens's 1,527 test images; final judgments use Gemini 3.7 Flash against private references. The paper does not report reviewer-human agreement or test metrics broken down by the twelve error types.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: RATED: Reliability-Aware AI Agent Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics
titleEn: RATED: Reliability-Aware Tool Retrieval for AI Agents via Execution Dynamics
summary: RATED is a tool retrieval framework for AI agents that combines semantic matching with dynamic reliability adaptation, using a lightweight contextual bandit module to rerank candidates based on real-time execution feedback, adapting to runtime tool failures without retraining. On the EcoAgent benchmark with 5,172 real tools, its MRR improves by 52.2% relative to the ToolLLM API retriever, and under severe API failures with a 30% failure rate, the failure selection rate drops from 86.2% to 2.9%, with additional latency under 1 ms.

parts.text: The agent must select tools from a growing tool library that remain usable at execution time. Existing retrieval mainly optimizes semantics; the authors claim that methods updating the planner with batch trajectories cannot change ranking between adjacent requests. The authors claim that over 50% of tools in four platform catalogs have broken links or lack authentication.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: RATED uses a contrastively fine-tuned and frozen DRAGON dual encoder to take the top-10 by semantic score, then reranks with a per-tool discounted LinUCB based on binary feedback from single executions and a metadata prior. EcoAgent contains 5,172 tools, and synthetic queries are generated by Gemma-3-1b.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Under 30% failure injection, RATED's FSR is 2.9%, and ToolLLM's is 86.2%. On EcoAgent-Real, the authors report a 52.2% MRR improvement relative to ToolLLM, but 0.618 is lower than Ada-002's 0.670. The extra latency is 0.172 ms.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: Conclusion leaves cold-start evaluation of newly added tools and live agent runtime validation as future work. Experiments include EcoAgent offline retrieval, and dynamic selection under simulated persistent failures at 20% and 30%. The paper does not report the number of repetitions for the dynamic experiments.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: FAITH: Feasibility-Aware Safety-Filtered RL for High-Dimensional Systems
titleEn: FAITH: A feasibility-aware safety filtering reinforcement learning framework for high-dimensional systems
summary: FAITH is a model-free, feasibility-aware safe filtering reinforcement learning framework that uses a feedforward network to approximate the optimal state-action safety value and amortizes minimal intervention filtering, allowing the task policy to optimize reward through the filtered dynamics without adding competing safety terms in policy updates. On a double integrator, Safety Gym, and a 29-DoF humanoid robot, FAITH achieves no violations and the highest reward from feasible starting points, reaching a 99.95% safety rate in Walking-Avoid while retaining 97% of the unfiltered reward, and achieving the highest safety rate in Push-Avoid by sacrificing balance and falling away from the protected zone; the same policy is also demonstrated on a real Unitree G1 humanoid robot.

parts.text: Safe reinforcement learning often places safety and task return in the same policy objective, and updates may cancel each other out. Classical filters require analytic safety functions and dynamics and only minimize instantaneous action deviation; projection is undefined when no safe action exists. High-dimensional contact systems also need to distinguish whether violations can ultimately be avoided.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: FAITH uses a backup actor and safety critic to approximate the optimal state-action peak harm, then amortizes minimal intervention with a feedforward residual network. The task policy uses PPO to maximize task reward only on filtered dynamics. When the acceptance set is empty, the same loss prioritizes lower predicted peak harm, without switching to a recovery controller.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: On feasible starting points in the double integrator and Safety Gym, FAITH achieves 100% safety rate, and the authors claim the highest reward among violation-free methods. Walking-Avoid safety rate 99.95%, the authors claim retaining 97% of unfiltered reward; Push-Avoid safety rate 85.45%, the highest measured.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors note that with discounting, finite λ, and learning errors, there are no formal safety or optimality guarantees; evaluation is limited to planar protected zones, excluding impact severity and human injury. Hardware demonstrations are qualitative, with no safety or harm statistics. Simulation covers the double integrator, SafetyCarCircle1-v0, and two 29-DoF tasks.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: GROB 用公开网络痕迹研究自主智能体活动归因边界
Tracing and Taming Hallucinated Terms via Subsequence-Association Filtering and Breadth-Aware Selection for LLM Query Expansion
titleEn: Using subsequence association filtering and breadth-aware selection to suppress hallucinated words in LLM query expansion
summary: SAFE-QE suppresses hallucinated words in LLM query expansion through subsequence association filtering and breadth-aware selection. On TREC and BEIR, its nDCG@10 is not statistically different from generative and corpus-guided expansion, but it injects 4.3 unsupported words per query, while Query2doc and HyDE inject 27.8 and 57.5. The method is training-free and retriever-agnostic, scores candidate words by cross-context reproducibility conditioned on the corpus, down-weights words that recur under random contexts but lack support from pseudo-relevance sets, and proposes the Hallucinated Expansion Term Rate to measure query-side faithfulness.

parts.text: LLM query expansion can inject entities unsupported by the corpus and off-topic words, increasing ranking noise and potentially harming strong retrievers. Existing filtering typically keeps or discards words based on co-occurrence with retrieval evidence, and how many words to keep is left to fixed top-k or tuned weights.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: SAFE-QE does not train. After sampling candidate terms with an open instruction-tuned LLM, it scores them using reproducibility across random contexts and support from pseudo-relevant documents, penalizing terms that are highly reproducible and unsupported; then it greedily maximizes coverage under grounding constraints and filters by resampling frequency. It also defines a query-side HETR.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: In Table 1, except for the no-expansion row, corrected p > 0.5 for nDCG@10 vs. HyDE, CSQE, MILL; Query2doc p = 0.021. Table 3 macro-average: SAFE-QE unsupported word load 4.79, Query2doc 27.83, HyDE 57.47.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors state that τg is fixed and should be calibrated per retriever, component ablations were not done, and limited-sample analysis of breadth and consistency remains open. The experiments use six collections, three retrievers, and four generators; the paper does not report the values of each hyperparameter.
parts.label: Limitations and future work
